passage_text: Researchers investigated the effect of a novel antihypertensive agent on systolic blood pressure (SBP) in adults with stage 1 hypertension. The study enrolled 120 participants, stratified into four age groups (18–29, 30–39, 40–49, 50–59 years). All participants received the drug once daily for four weeks. Baseline SBP and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) were recorded, and follow‑up measurements were taken at the end of the study period. The investigators reported mean SBP reductions and calculated the percent change from baseline for each age group. The results suggested that younger adults experienced a greater relative reduction in SBP compared to older adults, although absolute reductions were similar across groups. The study concluded that the drug is effective across age ranges, with a slightly enhanced relative benefit in younger patients.
stem: Which age group achieved the greatest percent reduction in systolic blood pressure?
explanation: The 18–29 age group had a 14.5% reduction, which is the highest among all groups.
trap: Choosing the 50–59 group because it has the highest baseline and follow-up SBP values, confusing raw blood pressure with percent reduction (it actually has the smallest, 13.2%).

stem: Which study design best controls for age-related confounding when evaluating the drug’s efficacy?

options.B: Randomized controlled trial with age‑matched groups
options.C: Case‑control study selecting only younger participants
options.D: Observational cohort study without age adjustment

explanation: Randomization with age‑matched groups balances age as a confounder, providing the strongest control for age-related effects.
trap: A cross‑sectional design inherently eliminates confounding by age.

stem: Which statement is NOT supported by the data presented in the passage?

options.A: Percent reductions ranged from 13.2% to 14.5% across the age groups.
options.B: Younger adults experience a greater relative reduction than older adults.
options.C: Absolute reductions in systolic blood pressure are similar across age groups.
options.D: The drug is ineffective in adults over 50 years old.

explanation: Correct: D) In the 50-59 group mean SBP fell from 144 to 125 mmHg (19 mmHg, 13.2%), so the data show a reduction and give no support for 'ineffective'. Why the others are wrong: A) The table lists 14.5, 13.6, 13.4 and 13.2%. B) The youngest group had 14.5% versus 13.2% in the oldest. C) Absolute reductions were 20, 19, 19 and 19 mmHg.
trap: Reading the slightly smaller percent reduction in the oldest group as no effect at all, when the table shows a 19 mmHg (13.2%) fall.

stem: All participants in this study received the drug and there was no placebo group. Which conclusion is justified by the table?

options.A: The drug, rather than a placebo effect, caused the SBP reductions.
options.B: Mean SBP was lower at 4 weeks than at baseline in every age group.
options.C: The drug lowers SBP more than a placebo does.
options.D: Age determines how much the drug lowers SBP.

explanation: Correct: The table lists a lower mean SBP at 4 weeks than at baseline in all four groups (138 to 118, 140 to 121, 142 to 123, 144 to 125). Why the others are wrong: A) with no placebo group, a placebo effect or other time-related change cannot be excluded, so causation is not shown. C) no comparison with placebo was made. D) absolute reductions are 19-20 mmHg in every group and no test of age as a determinant is reported.
trap: Treating a before-and-after drop in a single-arm study as proof that the drug caused it.
